# Day 11: RNNs, (Bi)LSTM, GRUs

## Learning goals

By the end of this session you should be able to explain why a hidden
state carried across sequence positions suits variable-length
sequential data better than a fixed-size window; explain why
backpropagation through many time steps tends to vanish or explode, and
how LSTM's gates address it; describe what a bidirectional RNN and a
GRU each change relative to a plain LSTM, and why; and describe, using
the real history of a real bioinformatics tool, how protein sequence
models moved from feedforward networks through this day's RNN/LSTM
family and on toward pretrained protein language models.

## Recurrent processing: a hidden state carried through time

Every model so far in this course sees a fixed-size input: Day 8-9's
one-hot subcellular-localization vector, Day 10's 1D-CNN's fixed
receptive field. Real biological sequences vary in length, and — for a
genuinely sequential problem like predicting the next value in a time
series or labelling a protein residue by residue — the right answer at
one position can depend on everything that came before it, arbitrarily
far back. A **recurrent neural network (RNN)** handles this by carrying
a **hidden state** $h_t$ forward one position at a time, updated at
each step from the current input and the previous hidden state:

$$
h_t = \tanh(W_{xh} x_t + W_{hh} h_{t-1} + b_h)
$$

Unlike a CNN's fixed kernel width, this hidden state can in principle
carry information from arbitrarily far back in the sequence — the same
weights $W_{xh}$, $W_{hh}$ are reused at every position, so an RNN
naturally handles sequences of any length with a fixed number of
parameters.

### Why gradients vanish or explode through time

Training an RNN means backpropagating through every time step it
processed — **backpropagation through time (BPTT)**. Conceptually this
is the same chain rule as any other network, but now the same
recurrent weight matrix $W_{hh}$ gets multiplied into the gradient once
per time step. Whether that repeated multiplication shrinks or grows
depends on the weight matrix's eigenvalues: an eigenvalue below 1
shrinks the gradient toward zero over many steps (**vanishing**); above
1, it grows without bound (**exploding**) — the same real problem Day 9
already ran into with a 6-layer *feedforward* network, now happening
along the *sequence length* instead of network depth:

![Repeated multiplication by a fixed factor, over many recurrent steps. At factor 0.8, the signal shrinks to about $1.5\times10^{-6}$ of its start after 60 steps; at factor 1.2, it grows to about $5.6\times10^4$.](figs/day11-vanishing-exploding.png){width=85%}

A long protein sequence, or a long time series, can easily need
hundreds of recurrent steps — more than enough for even a mild
eigenvalue away from 1 to vanish or explode completely.

## LSTM: gates and the Constant Error Carousel

**Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)** fixes this with the same idea Day 9's
skip-connection-flavored fixes used: give the gradient a path that
doesn't require repeated multiplication. LSTM keeps a separate **cell
state** $c_t$, updated *additively* rather than by repeated
multiplication, controlled by three gates — forget ($f_t$), input
($i_t$), and output ($o_t$):

$$
f_t = \sigma(W_f[h_{t-1}, x_t]), \quad i_t = \sigma(W_i[h_{t-1}, x_t]), \quad \tilde c_t = \tanh(W_c[h_{t-1}, x_t])
$$
$$
c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde c_t, \qquad o_t = \sigma(W_o[h_{t-1}, x_t]), \qquad h_t = o_t \odot \tanh(c_t)
$$

When the forget gate is close to 1 and the input gate close to 0,
$c_t \approx c_{t-1}$: the cell state passes through almost unchanged,
sidestepping the vanishing-gradient multiplication above — this
mechanism is sometimes called the **Constant Error Carousel**. It's why
LSTM's forget-gate bias is conventionally initialized to $+1$ at the
start of training, favoring "remember" by default (verified in the
notebook: a from-scratch `ExplicitLSTMCell`, matched exactly against
PyTorch's own `nn.LSTMCell` on identical weights).

## Bidirectional LSTM and GRU

Two real refinements on plain LSTM, both used in this day's own case
study below:

- **Bidirectional (BiLSTM)**: runs one LSTM left-to-right and a second
  right-to-left over the same sequence, concatenating their hidden
  states at each position. Whether a residue is part of a signal
  peptide (this day's case study) depends on context from *both*
  directions — a forward-only LSTM can only see what came before a
  given position, never what comes after.
- **GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit)**: merges LSTM's three gates into two (a
  reset gate and an update gate) and drops the separate cell state,
  folding everything into a single hidden state — fewer parameters,
  often comparably good in practice.

Whether BiLSTM or GRU actually helps on a real task is an empirical
question, answered directly below rather than asserted.

- Wikipedia, [Long short-term memory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_short-term_memory) and [Gated recurrent unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gated_recurrent_unit) — full gate equations and variants beyond what's needed here
- d2l.ai, [Modern Recurrent Neural Networks](https://d2l.ai/chapter_recurrent-modern/index.html) — LSTM, GRU, and deep/bidirectional RNNs in full mechanical detail

## Case study: SignalP — from feedforward networks to protein language models

**Signal peptides** are short N-terminal sequences (a hydrophobic core
flanked by an n-region and a c-region) that direct a protein for
secretion — discovered by Günter Blobel, who won the 1999 Nobel Prize
in Physiology or Medicine for it. Predicting whether, and where, a
protein has one is a real **sequence-labelling** task: a label per
residue, not one label per protein — exactly what this day's recurrent
models are built for.

**SignalP**'s own 30-year history is a real, concrete tour through this
entire course's model-architecture arc, not a hypothetical one:

| Version | Year | Architecture |
|---|---|---|
| SignalP 1.0 | 1995 | Feedforward ANN, one hidden layer, sliding windows |
| SignalP 4.0 | 2011 | Feedforward ANN, nested cross-validation, redefined negative set |
| SignalP 5.0 | 2019 | **CNN + RNN (LSTM) + CRF** |
| SignalP 6.0 | 2022 | **ProtBERT (Transformer protein language model) + CRF** |

SignalP 5.0 used exactly this day's toolkit — a CNN feeding an LSTM,
with a conditional random field (CRF) layer replacing the older
hand-designed C-score/S-score post-processing. SignalP 6.0 then
replaced the LSTM component with a pretrained Transformer-based protein
language model (more on what that means below), fine-tuned for the
task — the same recurrent-to-attention transition Day 12 covers in
general.

One more detail, from the SignalP authors' own account of version 1.0:
its training software had a "spell-checking" mode that erased the
middle amino acid in a window and trained the network to predict it
from the ones around it — masked-residue prediction, in 1995,
"presumably represent[ing] the first machine learning language model in
the domain of biological sequence analysis," in the authors' own words.
The idea this day's protein-language-model section closes with is
older than it might seem.

### Real comparison: sliding-window baseline vs. SimpleRNN vs. LSTM vs. BiLSTM vs. GRU

The notebook fetches a live signal-peptide dataset from UniProtKB
(reviewed entries with a `ft_signal` annotation) and trains all five
models on the identical residue-labelling task — N-terminal 70
residues, predicting signal-peptide membership per position:

![Signal-peptide residue detection: a sliding-window logistic baseline against SimpleRNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, and GRU taggers, and the corresponding precision-recall curves. BiLSTM wins clearly on every threshold-dependent metric.](figs/day11-model-comparison.png){width=100%}

| Model | Params | Precision | Recall | F1 | MCC | AUPR | AUROC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sliding window | — | 0.296 | 0.888 | 0.444 | 0.460 | 0.588 | 0.941 |
| SimpleRNN | 4,105 | 0.680 | 0.287 | 0.404 | 0.418 | 0.538 | 0.935 |
| LSTM | 14,761 | 0.733 | 0.239 | 0.361 | 0.398 | 0.578 | 0.947 |
| **BiLSTM** | 29,017 | 0.775 | 0.476 | **0.590** | **0.587** | **0.714** | **0.972** |
| GRU | 11,209 | 0.733 | 0.350 | 0.474 | 0.484 | 0.611 | 0.951 |

A real, non-forced result: BiLSTM clearly wins on every
threshold-dependent metric (F1, MCC, AUPR) and on AUROC, exactly
matching the argument above — a forward-only model genuinely loses
information a bidirectional one can use, on this real task. Plain LSTM,
notably, does *not* beat the much simpler sliding-window baseline on
F1/MCC here (it trades recall for precision) — a reminder that gating
alone doesn't guarantee a win; direction of context mattered more than
the gates did for this particular dataset.

## Protein language models: the same building blocks, pretrained at scale

**UniRep** (Alley, Khimulya, Biswas, AlQuraishi & Church, *Nature
Methods* 2019) is a real protein language model built on exactly this
day's own toolkit — a **multiplicative LSTM (mLSTM)**, trained by
next-amino-acid prediction on roughly 24 million UniRef50 sequences.
No labels, no annotation: the model just learns to predict the next
residue given the ones before it, the same self-supervised idea behind
GPT-style language models, but built on an LSTM rather than a
Transformer. The resulting fixed-length representations turned out
useful for predicting secondary structure, stability, and function —
this is what "protein language model" means at the
representation-learning level, using only the recurrent machinery this
day already covers.

SignalP 6.0 (above) shows the next step directly: the same task,
upgraded from this day's architecture family (5.0's LSTM) to a
Transformer-based protein language model (6.0's ProtBERT). A second,
more recent example: **ProstT5** ([Heinzinger et al.](https://github.com/mheinzinger/ProstT5),
TU Munich/Rost lab) is a T5-based (Transformer) protein language model
that translates between amino-acid sequence and 3Di structure tokens
(Foldseek's structural alphabet) — a real, current example of what a
protein language model can do, described here purely at the level of
*what it does*.

**How Transformer-based models like ProtBERT and ProstT5 actually work
internally — self-attention — is Day 12's job, not this one.** This
section is deliberately about the *concept* (pretrain on massive
unlabeled sequence data, get useful representations out) using
examples architecturally connected to this day, not a preview of the
mechanism.

## The notebook

`notebooks/day11-rnns-lstm-gru-in-code.ipynb` verifies every claim above
in code: the vanishing/exploding-through-time plot, a from-scratch
`ExplicitLSTMCell` checked exactly against PyTorch's own `nn.LSTMCell`,
and the real SignalP case study — a live UniProtKB fetch, a
sliding-window baseline, and a shared `SeqTagger` class switched between
SimpleRNN, LSTM, BiLSTM, and GRU, with every number in the comparison
table above read back from the notebook's actual executed output.
Adapted from this repo's own `notebooks/ch09.ipynb`, `ch10.ipynb`, and
`ch10_signal_peptide_detection.ipynb` (the last of which already builds
the SignalP dataset fetch and the SlidingWindow/SimpleRNN/LSTM
comparison this notebook extends with BiLSTM and GRU). Open it in
[Google Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/github/ElofssonLab/kb8029-book/blob/main/notebooks/day11-rnns-lstm-gru-in-code.ipynb)
via the badge at the top of the notebook page to edit and run it
yourself.
